techniques.name: Box Breathing
techniques.summary: Four even counts give you a steady rhythm and a simple focus before a stressful moment.
techniques.mechanism:
Box breathing can help you feel composed by slowing the breath and giving your attention one clear task.

• Equal counts keep the rhythm steady and easy to follow.
• Two comfortable pauses slow the cycle without asking for a very long breath.
• Counting can interrupt the mental rehearsal that often builds before pressure.

mechanismContent.lead: Box breathing can help you feel composed by slowing the breath and giving your attention one clear task.
items: Equal counts keep the rhythm steady and easy to follow.
Two comfortable pauses slow the cycle without asking for a very long breath.
Counting can interrupt the mental rehearsal that often builds before pressure.

techniques.evidence:
Research is growing, though it does not show that the square pattern is uniquely effective.

• A 2023 trial included box breathing among daily five-minute practices followed for a month.
• The breathing groups reported improvements in mood, with the clearest results for cyclic sighing.
• This does not establish that equal counts or holds are needed to feel calmer.

techniques.name: Coherent Breathing
techniques.summary: A smooth, even rhythm can help your body settle over a few quiet minutes.
techniques.mechanism:
Coherent breathing can help the rhythms of your breath, heart and blood pressure work together more smoothly.

• Your heart speeds up as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out.
• At this pace, those changes can line up with the slower rhythm of blood pressure.
• The effect builds over minutes, making this a useful exercise when you have time to settle.

techniques.evidence:
This is one of the best-studied patterns in the catalogue, with some important limits.

• Reviews of slow paced breathing find small to medium reductions in stress and anxiety.
• A blinded trial of about 400 people found no advantage over breathing at 12 breaths per minute.
• That trial used ten minutes a day for four weeks, longer than this exercise's default session.

techniques.name: 4-7-8 Breathing
techniques.summary: A very slow 4-7-8 rhythm can give a busy mind something simple to follow as you wind down.
techniques.mechanism:
4-7-8 breathing can help you slow down at the end of the day by stretching each round to about 19 seconds.

• The long breath out makes the very slow pace easier to maintain.
• The hold and the counting keep your attention on three simple tasks.
• Shorten every part if the hold feels strained. A comfortable rhythm matters more than the exact count.

Shorten every part if the hold feels strained. A comfortable rhythm matters more than the exact count.

techniques.evidence:
The wider evidence supports slow breathing, but not the special power of the 4-7-8 counts.

• A 2026 trial in people with tinnitus reported improvements in sleep and psychological symptoms.
• Results in that clinical group do not establish a sleep benefit for healthy people.
• The evidence does not establish these exact counts as the best way to wind down.

techniques.name: Extended Exhale
techniques.summary: A gentle four-in, six-out rhythm can make slow breathing easy to follow without a hold.
techniques.mechanism:
Extended Exhale can help you settle into a slow rhythm without the effort of a breath hold.

• A four-in, six-out cycle gives you six breaths per minute.
• The longer breath out is often the easiest part of the cycle to stretch comfortably.
• The simple ratio suits you whether you feel wound up or nearly asleep.

The simple ratio suits you whether you feel wound up or nearly asleep.

techniques.evidence:
Research supports the slow pace more clearly than the longer breath out.

• A 2024 study of more than 800 people linked slower breathing with feeling calmer.
• A 12-week trial found no clear stress benefit from a longer breath out compared with equal counts.
• The longer breath out may still be useful because it makes a slow rhythm easier to follow.

techniques.name: Physiological Sigh
techniques.summary: One or two double breaths in, then a long breath out, give you a brief pause during a stressful moment.
techniques.mechanism:
A physiological sigh pairs a second small sip of air with a longer breath out.

• Keep both breaths in gentle rather than trying to fill your lungs as much as possible.
• Let the longer breath out finish without forcing it.
• You can use your nose or mouth to breathe out, whichever feels comfortable.

techniques.evidence:
Research on a longer sighing practice does not establish the effect of one or two sighs.

• A 2023 trial tested five minutes a day, not this quick reset.
• That study's mood findings cannot be assumed for this much shorter exercise.
• Treat this as a brief breathing prompt, not a proven treatment for anxiety.

techniques.name: Cyclic Sighing
techniques.summary: Five minutes of soft, repeated sighs can turn a quick reset into a calm daily practice.
techniques.mechanism:
Cyclic sighing combines the release of a sigh with the steady pace of a five-minute daily practice.

• Each second sip is small; avoid trying to take the deepest possible breath.
• Ten-second cycles give you six breaths per minute, a pace often used in slow-breathing research.
• A mouth breath out may feel more natural. The trial used a mouth exhale; this app defaults to the nose.

A month-long trial provides encouraging evidence for a daily sighing practice, with limits.

• In 2023, five daily minutes were associated with improved mood and a lower resting breathing rate.
• The trial had about 30 people per group and came from one laboratory.
• The trial does not establish that this app's fixed timings or nasal exhale give the same results.

techniques.name: Pursed-Lip Breathing
techniques.summary: A gentle breath out through pursed lips can help you recover when you are already short of breath.
techniques.mechanism:
Pursed-Lip Breathing can make each breath feel more effective by keeping small airways open for longer.

• The narrow opening at your lips creates gentle pressure as you breathe out.
• That pressure can help trapped air leave before the next breath in.
• Let the air move steadily rather than blowing hard. The slower breath out is the useful part.

mechanismContent.lead: Pursed-Lip Breathing can make each breath feel more effective by keeping small airways open for longer.
items: The narrow opening at your lips creates gentle pressure as you breathe out.

Let the air move steadily rather than blowing hard. The slower breath out is the useful part.

techniques.evidence:
This is common in lung care, but the average benefit is small.

• A 2024 review covered 73 trials of several breathing methods, mainly in people with lung disease.
• For pursed-lip or diaphragmatic breathing, the average breathlessness change was below the review's threshold for a meaningful clinical benefit.
• Healthy people are rarely studied, so claims about general calm are uncertain.

techniques.preparation: Part your lips gently, as though you were about to whistle or cool a spoonful of soup.

preparationContent.lead: Part your lips gently, as though you were about to whistle or cool a spoonful of soup.

techniques.name: Humming Breath
techniques.summary: A steady hum on each long breath out can make slow nasal breathing feel grounded and absorbing.
techniques.mechanism:
Humming Breath can give a slow rhythm a soothing sound and a physical vibration you can follow.

• Humming makes the air in the nose and sinuses vibrate.
• It briefly raises measured nitric oxide in the nose; that is not proof of a health benefit.
• The hum naturally keeps the breath out slow and nasal without extra counting.

It briefly raises measured nitric oxide in the nose; that is not proof of a health benefit.
The hum naturally keeps the breath out slow and nasal without extra counting.

techniques.evidence:
The effect on nasal nitric oxide is well established; the wider wellbeing claims are less certain.

• A small 2002 experiment measured much higher nasal nitric oxide during humming than quiet exhalation.
• This measured a physical response, not relief from anxiety or improved sleep.
• The evidence cited here does not establish humming as a treatment for sinus infections.

techniques.name: Cooling Breath
techniques.summary: A gentle mouth breath in and nasal breath out can feel refreshing when heat makes it hard to settle.
techniques.mechanism:
Cooling Breath can create a refreshing sensation by drawing air slowly across the moisture in your mouth.

• A curled tongue or gently closed teeth can both create the cooling airflow.
• Breathing out through the nose returns you to a slow, comfortable rhythm.
• Choose another exercise in cold or polluted air, or if cool air makes your chest feel tight.

techniques.evidence:
Research is limited, especially on whether the exercise cools more than your mouth.

• One unblinded trial of about 100 people tracked blood pressure and heart rate variability (HRV) for three months.
• That trial studied people with high blood pressure, not whole-body cooling in healthy people.
• A cool feeling in your mouth does not show that your body temperature has fallen.

techniques.name: Bellows Breath
techniques.summary: A short round of quick nose breathing can feel stimulating, but benefits for energy and focus are uncertain.
techniques.mechanism:
Bellows Breath can create a quick, bright sense of energy by copying the breathing pattern of exertion.

• Fast, forceful breathing can raise heart rate and adrenaline.
• It also lowers carbon dioxide quickly, which can cause tingling or lightheadedness.
• Keep the bout brief and stay seated. Stop and breathe normally if you feel lightheaded or tingly.

techniques.evidence:
Small studies of traditional fast breathing do not establish an energy or focus benefit for this short exercise.

• A 2018 study tested reaction time in 25 healthy women using several breathing and comparison conditions.
• Its 18-minute sessions differ substantially from this app's brief paced round.
• A stimulating feeling is not evidence of better attention or performance.

techniques.safetyNote: Sitting down only. Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly. Never in water, never while driving.

techniques.name: Wim Hof-style Rounds
techniques.summary: Three rounds of fast breathing and gentle holds can feel intense and focused when done safely.
techniques.mechanism:
Wim Hof-style rounds can feel vivid and absorbing because fast breathing changes the signals that normally end a breath hold.

• Thirty quick breaths lower carbon dioxide, which delays the urge to breathe.
• The same fast pace can raise adrenaline and cause a bright or tingling sensation.
• End every hold while it is still comfortable. A longer hold is not a better result.

End every hold while it is still comfortable. A longer hold is not a better result.

techniques.evidence:
A strong sensation does not establish a health benefit. Controlled research gives reason for caution.

• A 2024 blinded trial assigned 200 healthy young adults to fast breathing with long holds or a gentler breathing comparison.
• Both groups improved in stress, with no clear difference between them in stress or the other mental-health outcomes measured.
• The trial used 20 minutes daily for three weeks. It does not establish benefits for this app's exact sequence.

techniques.name: Long Box Breathing
techniques.summary: Longer counts make box breathing a calm way to focus before work.
techniques.mechanism:
Long Box Breathing can help gather your attention by making every side of the pattern deliberate.

• Six-count sides are long enough to need gentle attention rather than habit.
• The pauses give a wandering mind a clear count to return to.
• The slow, even rhythm can keep that concentration calm rather than tense.

• It does not establish an advantage over four-count box breathing.
• Treat the focus effect as how it may feel, not a proven change in attention.

techniques.name: Alternate-Nostril Breathing
techniques.summary: Slow breaths from side to side can settle you and focus your mind before work.
techniques.mechanism:
Alternate-Nostril Breathing can feel both calming and absorbing because each breath asks for a simple hand movement.

• Switching sides keeps your attention close to the breath.
• The slow nasal rhythm supports the same settling response as other slow exercises.
• After a few minutes, the sequence can become steady enough to carry into the task ahead.

2. Rest your ring finger beside your left nostril.

foundations.question: How exact does it need to be?
foundations.answer:
A comfortable exercise you repeat is more useful than a perfect pattern you avoid.

• Choose a well-studied exercise that feels easy enough to return to.
• Nose breathing, belly movement and exact counts are refinements you can add later.
• Treat fast breathing and long holds with extra care.

foundations.question: What should a good breath feel like?
foundations.answer:
A good breath feels quiet and comfortable. It does not need to be large.

• Let your ribs and belly move without forcing them.
• Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly.
• Shorten the count or stop if you feel short of air.

Shorten the count or stop if you feel short of air.

foundations.question: Is a deep breath always the answer?
foundations.answer:
No. A very large breath can make dizziness and air hunger worse when panic is rising.

• Try a smaller, quieter breath instead.
• Slow down only as far as feels comfortable.
• Breathing practice may support you, but it is not treatment for panic.

answerContent.lead: No. A very large breath can make dizziness and air hunger worse when panic is rising.

foundations.question: Why can slow breathing help?
foundations.answer:
Slow breathing supports the body systems that settle you.

• Your heart speeds up as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out.
• A slower cycle increases heart rate variability (HRV) while you practise.
• Many people feel calmer, but the effect is usually small.

A slower cycle increases heart rate variability (HRV) while you practise.
Many people feel calmer, but the effect is usually small.

foundations.question: Belly or chest?
foundations.answer: Let the breath move low if that feels easy. A hand below your ribs can help you notice the diaphragm working. Chest movement is not a mistake, and you never need to force your belly out.

answerContent.lead: Let the breath move low if that feels easy. A hand below your ribs can help you notice the diaphragm working. Chest movement is not a mistake, and you never need to force your belly out.

foundations.question: Nose or mouth?
foundations.answer:
Use your nose when it is comfortable, and use your mouth when it is not.

• Your nose filters, warms and moistens the air.
• Its gentle resistance can make the breath easier to slow.
• Nasal breathing does not add oxygen, and its wider benefits for healthy people remain uncertain.

foundations.question: How slow?
foundations.answer: Aim for slower than usual without straining. Five or six breaths per minute is the pace most often used in research. Shorten the count or breathe normally if the guide leaves you short of air.

answerContent.lead: Aim for slower than usual without straining. Five or six breaths per minute is the pace most often used in research. Shorten the count or breathe normally if the guide leaves you short of air.

foundations.question: What about fast breathing and holds?
foundations.answer:
Fast breathing and holds are optional, not more advanced versions of slow breathing.

• Fast breathing can lower carbon dioxide and cause tingling, dizziness or fainting.
• Practise it seated or lying down, never while driving or near water.
• Keep holds comfortable and skip them if you finish gasping.

foundations.question: How should I get comfortable?
foundations.answer:
Choose a position that suits the session.

• Sit to stay alert; lie down when preparing for sleep.
• Keep your posture easy rather than rigid, with your eyes open or closed.
• Follow the guide instead of the feeling if attention on your breath is uncomfortable, and stop early if needed.

foundations.question: How long and how often?
foundations.answer:
Start with a length you can repeat comfortably. A longer session is not automatically better.

• One minute may help with a momentary spike.
• Studies of change over time often use five-to-ten-minute sessions on most days.
• Research has not settled on one best dose.

foundations.question: When breathing itself is the problem
foundations.answer: An unsatisfying breath can have several causes, including a breathing-pattern problem. An app cannot tell you the cause. Seek medical advice if this is new or persistent, and urgent help if breathing is suddenly difficult, severe or accompanied by chest pain.

foundations.question: How good is the evidence?
foundations.answer:
The evidence is promising, modest and uneven.

• Trials find small to medium improvements in stress and anxiety, but many studies are small or at risk of bias.
• Slow breathing reliably changes heart rate variability (HRV) during practice; lasting benefits are less certain.
• No single pattern has proved best, and breathing practice should sit alongside medical treatment rather than replace it.

foundations.question: What do breathing numbers mean?
foundations.answer:
A breathing number describes one measurement, taken once.

• Comfortable-pause targets, coherence scores and breathing ages are not established measures of improvement.
• önd records what you practised, for how long, and how it felt.
• Optional leaderboards compare resting-rate results with other people; a ranking is not a measure of improvement.

occasions.name: Riding out a craving
occasions.summary: A few slow minutes can help take the edge off a craving while its peak passes.

progression.note: Start with four even counts, which are simple to follow on your first try.
Next, learn a quick reset for the moments when you cannot give five minutes.
Then turn the same sigh into a five-minute daily practice.
Then try a slow rhythm you can use lying down, with no hold to manage.
Finish with a smooth, count-free pace you can settle into for longer.
